questions.q: A lender uses an AI model to pre-screen loan applications. An audit finds that applicants with near-identical financial situations get different recommendations depending on their postcode. Which responsible AI principle is most directly at stake?
options: Fairness
Inclusiveness
Transparency
Reliability and safety
questions.explain: Fairness means similarly situated people get consistent outcomes, with no differing impact on comparable groups (the module uses loan applications as its example). Inclusiveness is about making AI accessible to everyone and letting everyone benefit, not about consistent decisions.

questions.q: A team adds screen-reader support, translation for small regional dialects, and an offline mode for users with poor connectivity to its AI product. Which responsible AI principle are they mainly addressing?
options: Inclusiveness
Fairness
Accountability
Transparency
questions.explain: Inclusiveness means AI systems work for and empower everyone, whatever their disability, language, or infrastructure. The module lists screen readers, regional dialects, and offline or low-connectivity operation as examples. Fairness is about consistent treatment in decisions, not access.

questions.q: An AI vendor publishes documentation that explains how its system works, justifies key design choices, states its known limitations, and enables logging and auditing. Which principle does this primarily put into practice?
options: Transparency
Accountability
Privacy and security
Reliability and safety
questions.explain: Transparency means AI systems are understandable: explain how they work, justify design choices, be honest about limitations, and support auditability. Accountability is related, but it is about people taking responsibility for how the system operates.

questions.q: Before training a model, a data team replaces customer names and account numbers with random identifiers but keeps each record separate. Which privacy technique are they using?
options: Pseudonymization
Aggregation
Envelope encryption
Data minimization
questions.explain: Pseudonymization replaces personal details with random identifiers. Aggregation would instead group records into summaries and remove individual-level detail. Data minimization means not collecting unnecessary data in the first place.

questions.q: A developer accepted a Copilot suggestion that later caused a security vulnerability in production. According to GitHub's responsible use guidance, who bears responsibility for that code?
options: The developer and team who accepted and shipped the code
GitHub, because its service generated the suggestion
The provider of the model that produced the suggestion
Nobody, since AI output is probabilistic by nature
questions.explain: GitHub's application card says users take on all risks of generated code, including security vulnerabilities, bugs, and IP infringement. That matches the accountability principle: people are accountable for AI systems and their output.

questions.q: Under deadline pressure, a developer starts accepting Copilot's proposed fixes without reading or testing them because they 'usually look right'. Which risk does GitHub's guidance describe here?
options: Overreliance on AI output
Hallucination in the model's output
Prompt injection
Training data bias
questions.explain: Overreliance is when users accept incorrect or incomplete AI output, often because mistakes are hard to spot. Hallucination describes the model producing plausible but false output. Here the risk lies in the user's behavior, not in the model's output.

questions.q: Copilot Chat confidently tells a developer to call a library method that does not exist in any version of that library. What is this behavior called?
options: Hallucination
Overreliance
Public code matching
Content filtering
questions.explain: A hallucination is output that sounds plausible but is factually wrong or made up. This is a known LLM risk and the reason human review matters. Overreliance describes the user accepting such output, not the model producing it.

questions.q: An organization wants to reduce the risk of unintended, harmful outcomes from the AI tools its developers use. Which approach does the module recommend?
options: Robust governance, transparent AI processes, and human oversight
Rely only on the vendor's built-in content filters for safety
Limit AI tool access to the most senior engineers on each product team
Allow AI completions but block every chat-based AI interaction
questions.explain: The module's mitigation advice is to put robust governance frameworks in place, make AI processes transparent, and include human oversight. Vendor filters help, but they don't replace governance and human review.

questions.q: Copilot produces a block of code that turns out to match code in a public repository. What does GitHub recommend before using it?
options: Treat it like any code you didn't write: test it, scan for IP issues, check security
Accept it as is, because public code on GitHub is free to reuse without restrictions
Rename the variables and functions so the code no longer counts as a match
Ignore the match, because Copilot only reproduces code under permissive licenses
questions.explain: GitHub says to take the same precautions as with any material you didn't independently originate: rigorous testing, IP scanning, and checking for security vulnerabilities. Public code can still carry license obligations, and renaming identifiers doesn't remove them.

questions.q: A team is using Copilot to help build a system that decides people's eligibility for health insurance. Which practice best follows GitHub's responsible AI guidance?
options: Add extra caution and human oversight; let affected people understand and appeal decisions
Let the AI-generated logic run unattended so that human bias is kept out of all the decisions
Turn off content filtering so the model has full freedom to reason about each applicant
Rely on Copilot's training data to guarantee fairness across every applicant group
questions.explain: Insurance and healthcare are consequential decisions in sensitive domains. GitHub advises caution, human oversight, and making sure affected people can understand decisions, appeal them, and update input data. Training data can contain bias, so it can't guarantee fairness.

questions.q: An AI system must keep behaving as designed when it meets unexpected inputs, and it must resist attempts to manipulate it into harmful behavior. Which principle does this describe?
options: Reliability and safety
Privacy and security
Transparency
Fairness
questions.explain: Reliability and safety means systems work as designed, respond safely to unexpected conditions, resist harmful manipulation, and minimize unintended harm. Privacy and security is about protecting data and access, not consistent behavior.

questions.q: A developer asks Copilot Chat in their IDE for advice on the tax implications of a contract clause and gets an odd answer. Based on GitHub's guidance, what is the best explanation?
options: Copilot Chat is designed for coding questions, so off-topic answers may be unreliable
Copilot Chat needs the Bing web search policy turned on before it will answer such questions
Copilot Chat must be told to act as a lawyer before it can answer legal questions
Copilot Chat only answers questions about files that are open in the editor
questions.explain: GitHub says Copilot Chat isn't designed for non-coding questions, and answers in those areas may be irrelevant or nonsensical. Its advice is to keep prompts on coding topics. A role prompt doesn't change what the tool is intended for.

questions.q: An organization on the GitHub Team plan wants to roll out Copilot with central seat management, organization-wide policies, and the ability to exclude sensitive files from Copilot. Which plan should the owner buy?
options: Copilot Business
Copilot Pro for each developer
Copilot Pro+ for each developer
Copilot Free with organization policies
questions.explain: Copilot Business is made for organizations and includes centralized management, policy control, and content exclusion. Owners of organizations on GitHub Free or GitHub Team can buy it. Individual plans (Free, Pro, Pro+) don't include content exclusion or organization-wide policy management.

questions.q: A company is considering Copilot Enterprise. Which platform requirement does GitHub list for this plan?
options: The enterprise uses GitHub Enterprise Cloud
Every organization is on the GitHub Team plan
An Azure subscription is linked to the enterprise
Each developer has an individual Copilot Pro plan
questions.explain: GitHub describes Copilot Enterprise as designed for enterprises using GitHub Enterprise Cloud, with all Copilot Business features plus more. Copilot Business is the plan that organizations on GitHub Free or GitHub Team can buy directly.

questions.q: A developer's company has a GitHub Enterprise license that includes the right to use Copilot, but the developer gets no Copilot access when they sign in to their IDE. What is the most likely missing step?
options: An administrator hasn't assigned them a Copilot seat
They haven't installed the Copilot CLI with npm
They need to first activate Copilot Free personally
Their repository hasn't been indexed by Copilot yet
questions.explain: To use Copilot at an organization's or enterprise's expense, an administrator must assign you a seat, even when the enterprise license includes Copilot. Copilot Free is only for individuals who don't get Copilot through an organization or enterprise.

questions.q: In VS Code on Windows, Copilot shows a gray inline suggestion. You'd like to compare it with other options without leaving the editor. What should you do?
options: Press Alt+] to cycle to the next suggestion
Press Ctrl+I to open inline chat and ask again
Press Esc, then retype the line more slowly
Run Copilot: Explain This from the context menu
questions.explain: Alt+] (Option+] on macOS) shows the next alternative suggestion, and Alt+[ shows the previous one. Tab accepts and Esc rejects. Ctrl+I opens inline chat, which is a different interaction.

questions.q: A developer wants to ask Copilot to refactor the function under the cursor and see the change right there in the editor, without switching to the Chat panel. Which feature fits best?
options: Inline chat, opened with Ctrl+I / Cmd+I
Copilot Spaces, opened from GitHub.com
Pull request summaries on GitHub.com
The command palette's Collect Diagnostics
questions.explain: Inline chat (Ctrl+I or Cmd+I) gives you a conversation tied to a specific code location, so you can request changes without switching context. Spaces is for curating project context for chat, not for in-place edits in the editor.

questions.q: A developer notices that Copilot gives few or no inline suggestions when they type well-known algorithms such as FizzBuzz, while it works fine on their own business logic. What is the most likely cause?
options: Suggestions matching public code are blocked by a policy
The editor's context window is full from other open tabs
The repository is private, so Copilot skips its files
Inline chat was disabled in the extension's settings
questions.explain: GitHub's docs note that limited or missing suggestions may mean duplication detection is on. When suggestions matching public code are blocked, common textbook implementations are the most likely to be suppressed. Private repositories still get suggestions.

questions.q: On a corporate network, Copilot fails with 'read ETIMEDOUT'. You want a quick test from the command line to see whether the machine can reach Copilot's servers. What should you run?
options: curl --verbose https://copilot-proxy.githubusercontent.com/_ping
git ls-remote https://github.com/github/copilot-docs.git HEAD
ping github.com and confirm that there is no packet loss
nslookup api.github.com to confirm the DNS resolution
questions.explain: GitHub's troubleshooting guide suggests a verbose curl to the _ping endpoint and expects an HTTP 200. You can add -x to route the request through your proxy. For Copilot Chat issues, test https://api.githubcopilot.com/_ping. A plain ICMP ping or DNS lookup doesn't test the HTTPS path Copilot uses.

questions.q: A developer's browser works through the corporate proxy, configured as https://proxy.corp.example:8443, but Copilot can't connect. Which explanation does GitHub's documentation support?
options: Copilot doesn't currently support proxy URLs that start with https://
Copilot needs a VPN instead of an HTTP proxy to reach its servers
Copilot supports proxy authentication only through OAuth tokens
Copilot always bypasses the proxy and connects to GitHub directly
questions.explain: Copilot connects to proxies with its own code, so a proxy setup your editor supports may not work for Copilot. GitHub specifically says proxy URLs starting with https:// aren't currently supported. Proxy authentication is supported with basic auth or Kerberos, not OAuth.

questions.q: Copilot reports 'unable to verify the first certificate' because the corporate proxy inspects TLS traffic. Which fix does GitHub recommend over the others?
options: Install the corporate CA in the OS trust store or have IT stop intercepting
Turn off Proxy Strict SSL permanently so all certificate errors are always ignored
Reinstall the Copilot extension to regenerate its bundled certificates
Switch to Copilot Free, which skips certificate validation by default
questions.explain: Recommended fixes are: install the custom certificates in the OS trust store, use a proxy that doesn't intercept secure connections, or ask IT to stop intercepting. Ignoring certificate errors (turning off Proxy Strict SSL) is possible, but GitHub warns it causes security issues and doesn't recommend it.

questions.q: Copilot in VS Code is misbehaving, but the GitHub Copilot output logs show no errors. Where should you look next?
options: Electron logs, via Developer: Toggle Developer Tools > Console
The repository's GitHub Actions logs for recent Copilot workflow runs
The organization audit log for Copilot seat assignment events
The Copilot usage metrics dashboard for the organization
questions.explain: In rare cases errors aren't logged in the usual places. Both GitHub and the module suggest viewing the Electron logs from the process running VS Code and the extension, using Toggle Developer Tools. Audit logs and metrics don't capture client-side extension errors.

questions.q: A team lead wants to gather the relevant repositories, specs, issues, and design notes in one place so that everyone's Copilot conversations about a new feature draw on the same curated context. Which feature fits?
options: Copilot Spaces
Copilot pull request summaries
Inline chat in the IDE
Copilot code review
questions.explain: Spaces let you organize repositories, code, issues, pull requests, notes, and files into a curated set of context. Copilot then uses that context to answer questions, and teams can share it. Pull request summaries only describe the changes in a single pull request.

questions.q: A developer finds Copilot's inline suggestions distracting when writing Markdown documentation, but wants to keep them for code. What is the simplest option in VS Code?
options: Use the Copilot status menu to disable completions for Markdown only
Uninstall the Copilot extension and reinstall it only for code workspaces
Ask an organization owner to add all Markdown files to content exclusion
Switch the account to a different plan that excludes Markdown files
questions.explain: When you disable completions from the Copilot status icon, VS Code asks whether to disable them globally or only for the current file's language. Content exclusion is an admin control for hiding sensitive files, not a way to set editor preferences.

questions.q: A developer prompts: 'Build the login page, set up the payment API, and also refactor the reporting module.' Results are vague and incomplete. Which of the 4 S's does this prompt break most clearly?
options: Single
Short
Surround
Specific
questions.explain: Single means each prompt should focus on one well-defined task or question. This prompt mixes three unrelated tasks. It also lacks detail, but the main problem is bundling several tasks into one request.

questions.q: Copilot's inline suggestions in 'helpers2.js' keep ignoring the project's existing data models, which are defined in other files that aren't open. Which change best follows the 'Surround' principle?
options: Open the related model files and use descriptive file names
Make each comment shorter so Copilot focuses on fewer words
Close every other tab so Copilot only sees the current file
Repeat the same comment several times to reinforce intent
questions.explain: Surround means giving Copilot rich context through descriptive file names and keeping related files open, because open tabs feed into suggestions. GitHub's docs also say to open relevant files and close only irrelevant ones.

questions.q: You paste one existing Celsius-to-Fahrenheit function into the prompt and ask Copilot to write a matching Fahrenheit-to-Kelvin function in the same style. Which approach is this?
options: One-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
Role prompting
questions.explain: One-shot prompting gives exactly one example so Copilot follows your patterns and conventions. Zero-shot gives no examples, and few-shot gives several.

questions.q: A developer needs a greeting function that handles morning, afternoon, evening, and edge cases at boundary times. They include several input/output examples in the prompt. What is the main benefit of this few-shot approach?
options: Several examples help Copilot handle multiple scenarios and edge cases
It turns off the model's foundational training in favor of the examples
It retrains the model so future prompts follow the same pattern
It skips content filtering because the examples are developer-written
questions.explain: Few-shot prompting gives several examples. It sits between zero-shot unpredictability and the precision of fine-tuning, and it is good for implementations that must handle multiple scenarios and edge cases. Examples guide this one response; they don't retrain the model.

questions.q: A developer wants a password validation function that follows OWASP guidance and guards against common attacks on the first try. Which prompting technique from the module fits best?
options: Role prompting, e.g. 'Act as a cybersecurity expert...'
Zero-shot prompting with just the function name typed
Chain prompting that repeats the full chat history each turn
Leaving the prompt vague so Copilot can pick the approach
questions.explain: Role prompting tells Copilot to act as a specific expert, such as a security, performance, or testing specialist. This brings domain expertise into the first draft, for example input sanitization and protection against common attacks, so fewer revisions are needed.

questions.q: After a long Copilot Chat session building an authentication module, a developer moves on to an unrelated caching feature. Answers start drifting and requests get more expensive. What is the best practice?
options: Start a new conversation and give a short, focused summary of the context
Keep the same thread so Copilot remembers everything discussed so far
Paste the full authentication code again in every new prompt for safety
Switch to inline suggestions only, since they don't use any context
questions.explain: Long histories add irrelevant context and cost more to process. Both the module and GitHub's docs recommend starting a new conversation for a new task, summarizing what matters, and referring to earlier work briefly instead of repeating it.

questions.q: You're writing a multi-line Copilot Chat prompt with a goal and several requirements. According to GitHub's guidance, how should you structure it?
options: State the broad goal first, then list requirements with the most important first
List edge cases first and put the overall goal at the very end of the prompt
Put every requirement into one long sentence so that Copilot weighs them all equally
Write the requirements as meta-rules such as 'Remember to always do X'
questions.explain: GitHub advises starting general and then getting specific, with the most important requirements first, because Copilot gives extra weight to the beginning and end of a prompt. It also advises stating rules directly instead of as meta-instructions.

questions.q: With a file open and its last response still on screen, a developer asks Copilot Chat 'What does this do?' and gets an explanation of the wrong thing. Which rewrite best fixes the issue?
options: What does the `createUser` function do?
Explain this again, but in much more detail.
Act as an expert and tell me what this does.
What does this do? Please answer carefully.
questions.explain: 'This' could mean the current file, the last response, or a specific block. GitHub advises avoiding ambiguity by naming exactly what you mean, such as a specific function or 'the code in your last response'.

questions.q: A developer asks Copilot in one prompt to 'generate a complete word-search puzzle game' and gets brittle, incomplete code. What should they do next?
options: Break it into small steps: build the grid first, then find words in it
Repeat the same prompt several times until a complete version appears
Make the prompt shorter, for example 'make word search', to cut ambiguity
Switch to few-shot prompting by pasting several complete word-search programs
questions.explain: GitHub uses this exact example: break a complex task into simple steps (generate a grid, find words in it, combine them, print results) and ask for them one at a time. Repeating the same prompt doesn't add any information.

questions.q: Copilot's first inline suggestion from a comment prompt is close but misses a requirement. Per the 'assert and iterate' practice, what is the most effective next step?
options: Remove the suggestion, add details and examples to the comment, then prompt again
Accept it as is and fix the remaining code by hand without involving Copilot
Delete the comment completely and start over with an unrelated new prompt
Keep pressing Tab repeatedly until Copilot eventually works out the missing requirement
questions.explain: The module recommends not starting from scratch. Instead, remove the suggestion, enrich your original comment with more detail and examples, and prompt again. GitHub's docs agree: iterate by refining the prompt, or keep the suggestion and ask for changes.

questions.q: A developer needs a date-parsing function with tricky format rules. Which approach from GitHub's prompt engineering guidance gives Copilot the clearest examples of expected behavior?
options: Have Copilot write unit tests first, then ask for a function that passes them
Ask for the function first and then let Copilot decide which tests are needed
Describe the format rules vaguely so Copilot can generalize more on its own
Ask Copilot to act as a date expert and skip giving any concrete examples
questions.explain: GitHub notes that unit tests can serve as examples: write tests for the function first, then ask Copilot to write a function those tests describe. Concrete examples (inputs, outputs, tests) reduce ambiguity far more than a role alone.

questions.q: In Copilot's prompt processing flow, which component blocks attempts to hack the prompt or trick the system into revealing how the model generates suggestions?
options: The proxy filter on a server in a GitHub-owned Azure tenant
The toxicity filter that screens out hate speech and personal data
The public code matching filter enabled by administrators
The Fill-in-the-Middle step that gathers code around the cursor
questions.explain: After context is gathered and the prompt is built, it goes to a proxy server in a GitHub-owned Microsoft Azure tenant. The proxy filters traffic and blocks prompt-hacking attempts. The toxicity filter targets harmful content and personal data, not prompt manipulation.

questions.q: A developer's prompt includes a customer's name, home address, and ID number. In the module's prompt flow, which step is responsible for filtering out this kind of data?
options: Toxicity filtering
The proxy filter
Fill-in-the-Middle pre-processing
Post-processing code quality checks
questions.explain: The toxicity filtering step blocks hate speech and inappropriate content, and also filters personal data such as names, addresses, and ID numbers. The proxy filter targets attempts to hack or manipulate the system.

questions.q: Copilot suggests code in the middle of a function that fits well with code both above and below the cursor. Which pre-processing technique makes this possible?
options: Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM)
LoRA fine-tuning
Few-shot prompting
Retrieval from the public code index
questions.explain: During context gathering, Copilot uses Fill-in-the-Middle to consider both the code before and the code after the cursor, which widens the model's view of the context. LoRA is a method for fine-tuning models, not a step that processes each prompt.

questions.q: Which of these happens in Copilot's outbound flow, after the LLM has generated a response but before the developer sees it?
options: Checks for issues like XSS or SQL injection and the optional public-code filter
Gathering filenames, open tabs, and code from before and after the cursor
Sending the developer's prompt and gathered context to GitHub's servers securely over HTTPS
Applying Fill-in-the-Middle to widen the context the model receives
questions.explain: In post-processing, the toxicity filter removes harmful content, then checks look for code quality and security problems such as XSS or SQL injection, plus the optional public-code filter. A response that fails is truncated or discarded. The other options are inbound steps.

questions.q: A security officer at a Copilot Business customer asks what happens to code context sent from the IDE to produce inline suggestions. Which statement is accurate?
options: The prompt is discarded once the suggestion is returned and isn't used to train models
The prompt is kept for 90 days and then used to fine-tune a customer-specific private model
The prompt is stored indefinitely in the repository's audit log for later review
The prompt is shared with the public code index to improve future suggestions
questions.explain: For code suggestions in the editor, Copilot doesn't keep prompts to train the foundational models and discards them once a suggestion is returned. For Business and Enterprise, IDE prompts and suggestions aren't retained by default.

questions.q: GitHub chose LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) over full fine-tuning to adapt LLMs. What is LoRA's main advantage?
options: It adds small trainable parts to each layer and leaves the original model unchanged
It retrains all of the model's parameters on the target dataset for best accuracy
It removes the need for any task-specific data by relying on prompts alone
It replaces the pretrained model with a smaller one built from scratch
questions.explain: Full fine-tuning trains every part of the network, which is slow and resource-heavy. LoRA adds smaller trainable components to each layer and keeps the original pretrained model as is, which saves time and compute.

cards.back: Fairness; reliability and safety; privacy and security; inclusiveness; transparency; accountability.

AI should treat everyone fairly, giving consistent outcomes to similarly situated people. Ways to mitigate bias include reviewing training data, testing with balanced demographic samples, adversarial debiasing, and monitoring results across user segments.

AI should work as designed, respond safely to unexpected conditions, and resist harmful manipulation. Safety means minimizing physical, emotional, and financial harm; reliability means consistent behavior without unwanted variability.

cards.front: Privacy and security practices from the module
cards.back: Get consent before collecting data, collect only what's needed, anonymize (pseudonymization or aggregation), and encrypt data in transit and at rest with protected keys (HSMs, secure vaults, envelope encryption).

AI should empower and be accessible to everyone, regardless of disability, language, or infrastructure. Examples: screen readers, captions, voice control, regional dialect support, and offline or low-connectivity operation.

Transparency: AI should be understandable, with clear explanations, justified design choices, honesty about limitations, and logging and auditing. Accountability: people, not the AI, are responsible for how the system operates and its impact.

Hallucination: the model produces plausible but false or made-up output. Overreliance: a user accepts incorrect or incomplete AI output, often because mistakes are hard to spot. Human review guards against both.

cards.front: Why Copilot quality varies by programming language
cards.back: Suggestion quality depends on how much varied training data exists for each language. Well-represented languages like JavaScript do best; less common languages may get lower-quality results.
Individual developers who don't have Copilot access through an organization or enterprise. It offers limited access to selected features and models (auto model selection only).

cards.front: Free Copilot access for students, teachers, and OSS maintainers
cards.back: Verified students can get Copilot Student at no cost. Verified teachers and maintainers of popular open source projects may be eligible for free Copilot Pro.

Business: for organizations and enterprises, with centralized management, policy control, and content exclusion. Enterprise: for enterprises on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, with all Business features plus a larger AI credit pool and extra enterprise capabilities.
Tab = accept, Esc = reject, Alt+] / Alt+[ = next/previous alternative (Option on macOS), Ctrl+Enter = open a tab with multiple suggestions.

cards.front: Common Copilot Chat slash commands (VS Code)
cards.back: /explain (explain code), /fix (propose a fix), /tests (generate unit tests), /fixTestFailure, /new (new project), /clear (new chat session), /help. Type / to see what's available.

cards.front: Where to find Copilot logs in VS Code
cards.back: View > Output, then choose GitHub Copilot in the dropdown. Or run 'Developer: Open Extension Logs Folder' to collect files for support. For more detail, set the log level to Trace with 'Developer: Set Log Level'.

Copilot uses its own proxy code. Proxy URLs starting with https:// aren't supported. Proxy authentication works with basic auth or Kerberos. Corporate proxies may also need company-level allowlisting.

cards.front: Code references for public-code matches (VS Code)
cards.back: If suggestions matching public code are allowed, accepting one adds an entry to the 'GitHub Copilot Log (Code References)' output, with the matching file URL and license (if found).
Single (one well-defined task), Specific (explicit, detailed instructions), Short (concise), Surround (descriptive file names and related files open for context).
Zero-shot: no examples, relies on the model's training (good for common patterns). One-shot: one example to copy conventions. Few-shot: several examples to handle multiple scenarios and edge cases.
Tell Copilot to act as a specific expert (security, performance, testing) to bring domain expertise into the first draft, e.g. 'Act as a cybersecurity expert...'.
Long histories add irrelevant context and cost more to process. Start a new conversation for a new task, summarize the relevant context, and refer to earlier work briefly instead of repeating it.

cards.front: Where to put key requirements in a prompt
cards.back: Start with the broad goal, then list specifics with the most important first. Copilot gives extra weight to the beginning and end of a prompt.
1) Prompt sent securely over HTTPS and context gathered (cursor code, file name and type, open tabs, project structure, languages, FIM). 2) Proxy filter. 3) Toxicity filter. 4) LLM generates code.
A proxy server in a GitHub-owned Microsoft Azure tenant that filters traffic and blocks attempts to hack the prompt or extract details about how the model generates suggestions.

The toxicity filter blocks hate speech, inappropriate content, and personal data. On the outbound side, it removes harmful generated content, then checks look for code quality and security problems (e.g. XSS, SQL injection) and apply the optional public-code filter. Failing output is truncated or discarded.
A pre-processing technique where Copilot considers code both before and after the cursor, so suggestions fit their surroundings.

Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model with a smaller task-specific dataset. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adds small trainable parts to each layer and leaves the original model unchanged, which saves time and resources.

cards.front: Context window limits: what to do
cards.back: The model can only process a limited amount of code and text at once. Break complex problems into smaller, focused prompts and include only the relevant code snippets.
